(S) R is simple · (N) R is right Noetherian · (Z) the centre k=Z(R) is infinite · (Hall​) Kdim(R/dR) is finite for every regular d∈R · (Hω​) KdimRR​≤ω.

Theorem A

PDF p. 2 · Lean graph

Assume (S), (N) and (Z). Let d∈R be regular with Kdim(R/dR) finite. Then for every nonzero a∈R, which may be a zero-divisor, and every B∈R there are H,U,V∈R with 1=dU+(B+Ha)dV. In particular R=dR+HdR for some H∈R.

Proof in the paper

Put I=dR, which contains the regular element d, and x=Bd, t=ad; then t=0 because a=0 and d is regular. Theorem A′ gives H with R=dR+(Bd+Had)R=dR+(B+Ha)dR, that is, 1=dU+(B+Ha)dV for some U,V∈R. For a=1 and B=0 this is R=dR+HdR.

Theorem A′

PDF p. 3 · Lean graph

Assume (S), (N) and (Z). Let I be a right ideal of R that contains a regular element and for which Kdim(R/I) is finite. Then for every x∈R and every nonzero t∈R there is H∈R with I+(x+Ht)R=R.

Proof in the paper

We prove by downward induction on e a statement that asks in addition for finitely many tests; each step uses the inductive hypothesis twice for the same ideal I and then combines the two answers with a generic central scalar. Let k=Z(R), let s∈I be regular and choose an integer N≥0 with Kdim(R/I)≤N. For 0≤e≤N+1 let P(e) be the assertion:

for every x∈R, every nonzero t∈R and every finite list L of tests there is H∈R such that f=x+Ht satisfies every test in L and KdimR/(I+fR)<e.

P(N+1) holds by Lemma 4.3, since R/(I+fR) is a quotient of R/I. We show that P(e+1) implies P(e) for 0≤e≤N; then P(0) holds, and P(0) with the empty list is Theorem A′, because KdimR/(I+fR)<0 means I+fR=R. Fix x, t and L.

Step 1 (a first element f). By P(e+1) there is H such that f=x+Ht satisfies L and J=I+fR has KdimR/J≤e.

Step 2 (torsion equation). By Goldie’s theorem there is a regular b with fb∈I (remark after Theorem 2.2). Then tb=0.

Step 3 (a correction g for the same ideal). The module R/J is Goldie-torsion, as s∈J, and KdimR/J≤e, so it has a unit test. Apply P(e+1) with x=0, the nonzero element tb and the list consisting of the unit test of R/J. This gives H2​ such that, with g=H2​t, the element H2​tb=gb satisfies KdimR/(J+gbR)<eandKdimR/Q≤e,where Q=I+gbR.(1)

Step 4 (an epic section modulo Q). Since I⊆J, we have J+gbR=I+fR+gbR=Q+fR. By (1) and Lemma 3.2 applied to Q, the section v=qQ​⋅f of R/Q is epic. Put u=qQ​⋅g.

Step 5 (a central scalar). By Lemma 4.2, applied to M=R/Q and to the tests in L, all but finitely many λ∈k make v+uλ epic and f+λg satisfy L. As k is infinite, choose such a λ=0.

Step 6 (inclusion). Put f′=f+λg and J′=I+f′R. Since λ is central, gbλ=f′b−fb∈J′,(2) because f′b∈f′R and fb∈I. As λ is a unit, gb∈J′, and hence Q+f′R=J′.

Step 7 (the dimension drops). As λ is central, qQ​⋅f′=v+uλ, which is epic. By Lemma 3.2, KdimR/(Q+f′R)<e, that is, KdimR/J′<e.

Step 8 (affine form). f′=x+(H+λH2​)t, and f′ satisfies every test in L. This proves P(e).

Corollary B

PDF p. 3 · Lean graph

Assume (S), (N), (Z) and (Hω​). Then the conclusion of Theorem A holds for every regular d∈R, and that of Theorem A′ for every right ideal that contains a regular element.

Proof in the paper

By Lemma 2.3, Kdim(R/I) is finite for every right ideal I containing a regular element, in particular for I=dR with d regular. Theorems A′ and A apply.

Corollary C

PDF p. 3 · Lean graph

Assume (S), (N), (Z) and (Hall​), for instance (Hω​).

(C.1)

Every finitely generated Goldie-torsion module M is cyclic. More precisely, for every x∈M and every nonzero t∈R there is h∈M with M=(x+ht)R.

(C.2)

Every right ideal I is generated by two elements. More precisely, there is a∈I such that every y∈I has a regular s with ys∈aR; and for every such a, every y∈I and every nonzero t∈R there is h∈I with I=aR+(y+ht)R.

Proof in the paper

By Lemma 2.3, (Hω​) implies (Hall​). Hence (C.1) is Proposition 6.1(b) by the remark after Lemma 2.3, and (C.2) is Proposition 6.2.

Proposition 6.1

PDF p. 12 · Lean graph

Assume (S), (N) and (Z).

(a)

Let c,u be Goldie-torsion elements of a module with Kdim(uR) finite. Then for every nonzero t∈R there is H∈R with cR+uR=(c+uHt)R.

(b)

Let M be a finitely generated Goldie-torsion module with KdimM finite. Then for every x∈M and every nonzero t∈R there is h∈M with M=(x+ht)R.

Proof in the paper

(a) We apply Theorem A′ to the annihilator of u. Choose a regular b with cb=0. The right ideal I1​={r∈R:ur=0} contains a regular element, and R/I1​≅uR has finite Krull dimension. Theorem A′ with x=0 and the nonzero element tb gives H and r∈R with 1−Htbr∈I1​, so that u=uHtbr. For z=c+uHt we get zbr=cbr+uHtbr=u, so u∈zR and c=z−uHt∈zR. Hence cR+uR=zR.

(b) We induct on the number m of generators u1​,…,um​ of M; for m=0 take h=0. The module M/u1​R is generated by m−1 elements and is Goldie-torsion with Kdim(M/u1​R)≤KdimM, so by induction there is y∈M with M=cR+u1​R for c=x+yt. By (a), as Kdim(u1​R)≤KdimM, there is H with cR+u1​R=(c+u1​Ht)R. Take h=y+u1​H.

Proposition 6.2

PDF p. 12 · Lean graph

Let R be simple and right Noetherian, and I a right ideal of R.

(a)

There is a∈I such that every y∈I has a regular s with ys∈aR.

(b)

Assume moreover (Z) and (Hall​). For every a as in (a), every y∈I and every nonzero t∈R there is h∈I with I=aR+(y+ht)R. In particular I is generated by two elements.

Proof in the paper

(a) We take for a the I-component of a regular element of the essential right ideal I⊕C. Choose a right ideal C maximal with I∩C=0, which exists as R is right Noetherian. The right ideal I⊕C is essential, since K∩(I⊕C)=0 for a right ideal K would give I∩(C+K)=0 and hence K=0 by the maximality of C; so by Goldie’s theorem it contains a regular element s=a+c with a∈I, c∈C, and sR is essential. Let y∈I. The right ideal {r∈R:yr∈sR} is essential: if K is a nonzero right ideal, either yK=0⊆sR, or yK is a nonzero right ideal and meets sR in some yr=0 with r∈K. So it contains a regular element s′, and ys′=sr′=ar′+cr′ for some r′. Then cr′=ys′−ar′∈I∩C=0, so ys′=ar′∈aR.

(b) The module I/aR is finitely generated by (N) and Goldie-torsion by the choice of a. By (Hall​) its Krull dimension is finite (Section 2). Proposition 6.1(b) applied to y+aR gives h∈I with I/aR=(y+ht+aR)R, that is, I=aR+(y+ht)R. For two generators take y=0 and t=1.

Theorem 7.4(a)

PDF p. 13 · Lean graph

Filtered rings. Let k be an infinite field and R a simple k-algebra with an exhaustive filtration such that grR is commutative Noetherian of classical Krull dimension at most m. Then R and Rop satisfy (N), (Z), KdimRR​≤m and KdimRRopop​≤m. Hence Theorems A′ and A and Corollary C hold for R and for Rop, for every regular d and every right, respectively left, ideal containing a regular element; in particular 1=Ud+Vd(B+aH) for some H,U,V, for every regular d, every nonzero a and every B. Moreover, for Goldie-torsion elements c,u of a right R-module and every nonzero t there is H with cR+uR=(c+uHt)R, and likewise for left modules.

Theorem 7.4(b)

PDF p. 13 · Lean graph

Weyl algebras. Let k be a field of characteristic zero and A=An​(k). For all nonzero d,a∈A and every B∈A there are H,U,V with 1=dU+(B+Ha)dV; in particular, for every nonzero d there are F,U,V with 1=dU+FdV, which is Stafford’s Conjecture 3.8. For every nonzero right ideal I, every x∈A and every nonzero t there is H with I+(x+Ht)A=A. Every finitely generated torsion right module M satisfies M=(x+ht)A, and every finitely generated torsion left module M satisfies M=A(x+th), for given x∈M, t=0 and some h∈M; in particular these modules are cyclic. If a is a nonzero element of a right ideal I, then for every y∈I and nonzero t there is h∈I with I=aA+(y+ht)A; similarly I=Aa+A(y+th) for left ideals; in particular one-sided ideals of A are generated by two elements.

Theorem 7.4(c)

PDF p. 13 · Lean graph

Differential operators. Let D=D(X) be as above. Every right and every left ideal of D is generated by two elements. For all nonzero d,a∈D and every B∈D there are H,U,V∈D with 1=dU+(B+Ha)dV, and H′,U′,V′∈D with 1=U′d+V′d(B+aH′); in particular, for every nonzero d there are F,U,V∈D with 1=dU+FdV. Every finitely generated torsion right module M satisfies M=(x+ht)D, and every finitely generated torsion left module M satisfies M=D(x+th), for given x∈M, t=0 and some h∈M.

Lemmas

§3 Germs

Definition 3.1

PDF p. 6

Let M and N be modules. A germ of level e from M to N is an equivalence class [U,φ] of homomorphisms φ:U→N defined on e-dense submodules U⊆M, where (U,φ) and (U′,φ′) are equivalent if φ and φ′ agree on some e-dense submodule contained in U∩U′. The germs form an abelian group Home​(M,N). The composite of [V,ψ]∈Home​(N,P) and [U,φ]∈Home​(M,N) is [φ−1(V),ψφ]. A germ [U,φ] is epic if N/φ(U) is e-small.

A definition: the Lean statements of the results that use it unfold it.

Lemma 3.2 unit germs

PDF p. 7 · Lean graph

Let J be a right ideal of R and r∈R. The germ qJ​⋅r of R/J is epic if and only if KdimR/(J+rR)<e. In particular qJ​ is epic.

Proof in the paper

The germ qJ​⋅r is the germ of the homomorphism R→R/J, y↦ry+J, whose image is (rR+J)/J and whose cokernel is R/(J+rR).

Lemma 3.3 critical germs

PDF p. 7
(a)

Every nonzero germ of level e between e-critical modules is invertible. In particular EC​ is a division ring for every e-critical module C.

(b)

Let M be a module with KdimM≤e and a critical series, and let C be e-critical. Then Home​(M,C) is a left EC​-vector space whose dimension is at most the number of top factors of the series; and if Home​(M,C)=0, then C is isomorphic, through an invertible germ, to one of the top factors.

Proof in the paper

(a) Let C,D be e-critical and [U,φ] a nonzero germ from C to D, with U⊆C e-dense. Then φ=0, so U=0 is e-critical. If kerφ=0, then φ(U)≅U/kerφ would be a nonzero e-small submodule of D; hence φ is injective. As φ(U)=0, it is e-dense in D, and [φ(U),φ−1] is a two-sided inverse of [U,φ]. The identity germ of C=0 is nonzero, so EC​ is a division ring.

(b) We induct on the length l of the series; for l=0 we have M=0. Let U=Ml−1​ and F=M/U. Restriction ρ([V,φ])=[V∩U,φ] is an EC​-linear map Home​(M,C)→Home​(U,C); here V∩U is e-dense in U because U/(V∩U) embeds in M/V. If ρ([V,φ])=0, then φ vanishes on an e-dense submodule W of U, so φ(V∩U) is a quotient of the e-small module (V∩U)/W and hence zero, as C has no nonzero e-small submodule. Then φ induces φ′:(V+U)/U→C on the e-dense submodule (V+U)/U of F, and [V,φ]↦[(V+U)/U,φ′] is an injective EC​-linear map kerρ→Home​(F,C) (it is well defined, since representatives that agree on an e-dense V3​ induce maps that agree on the e-dense (V3​+U)/U): if φ′ vanishes on an e-dense W′/U, then φ vanishes on V∩W′, which is e-dense in M. Hence dimHome​(M,C)≤dimHome​(U,C)+dimHome​(F,C), and Home​(M,C)=0 implies Home​(U,C)=0 or Home​(F,C)=0. If F is e-small, then F=0 and Home​(F,C)=0. If F is e-critical and y∈Home​(F,C) is nonzero, then y is invertible by (a), every z∈Home​(F,C) equals (z∘y−1)∘y, and so dimHome​(F,C)=1. The induction hypothesis for U completes the proof.

Lemma 3.4 epic criterion

PDF p. 8

Let M be a module with KdimM≤e, with a critical series whose top factors are C1​,…,Cm​, and let x∈Home​(N,M). Then x is epic if and only if for each i the map Home​(M,Ci​)→Home​(N,Ci​), h↦h∘x, is injective.

Proof in the paper

For the forward direction we show that a germ killed by x vanishes on an e-dense submodule; for the converse we build an e-critical quotient of M that x misses and map it to a top factor. Write x=[U,φ]. Suppose x is epic and h∘x=0 for h=[V,ψ]. Then ψφ vanishes on an e-dense W⊆φ−1(V), so ψ vanishes on φ(W). This submodule is e-dense in M, because M/φ(U) is e-small and φ(U)/φ(W) is a quotient of U/W; hence h=0.

Suppose x is not epic. Among the submodules P⊇φ(U) of M with M/P not e-small choose a maximal one, which is possible as M is Noetherian. Then Q′=M/P is e-critical: KdimQ′≤e, Q′ is not e-small, and Q′/Q′′ is e-small for every nonzero Q′′ by maximality. The projection p:M→Q′ is a nonzero germ, as its image Q′ is not e-small, and p∘x=0 since p vanishes on φ(U). By Lemma 3.3(b) there is an invertible germ a:Q′→Ci​ for some i, and h=a∘p is a nonzero element of Home​(M,Ci​) with h∘x=0.

Lemma 3.5 central scalars

PDF p. 8 · Lean graph

Let C be e-critical and λ in the centre Z(R) of R. Right multiplication by λ is an endomorphism of C; let ϕλ​∈EC​ be its germ. Then ϕλ​ lies in the centre of EC​, the map λ↦ϕλ​ is a ring homomorphism Z(R)→Z(EC​), and w⋅λ=ϕλ​∘wfor all w∈Γe​(C).

Proof in the paper

If ψ:V→C represents a germ in EC​, then Vλ⊆V and ψ(vλ)=ψ(v)λ, so ψ commutes with ϕλ​. The map λ↦ϕλ​ is multiplicative and additive. If ψ:U→C represents w with U⊆R a right ideal, then for y∈U we have λy=yλ∈U and ψ(λy)=ψ(yλ)=ψ(y)λ, so w⋅λ and ϕλ​∘w agree on U.

Lemma 3.6 pencils

PDF p. 8

Let E be a division ring, F a field and κ:F→E a ring homomorphism with central image. Let D,W be left E-vector spaces with dimE​D<∞ and P,P′:D→W be E-linear, and call the family of E-linear maps P+κ(λ)P′, λ∈F, a pencil.

(i)

If P is injective, then P+κ(λ)P′ is injective for all but finitely many λ∈F.

(ii)

If P′ is injective, then P+κ(λ)P′ is injective for all but finitely many λ∈F.

Proof in the paper

(i) As E is a division ring and dimE​D<∞, P has an E-linear retraction π:W→D. The value λ=0 is good. If λ=0 and (P+κ(λ)P′)(v)=0 with v=0, then πP′(v)=−κ(λ)−1v, so v is an eigenvector of πP′ for the central eigenvalue −κ(λ)−1. Since κ is injective, distinct bad λ give distinct central eigenvalues, and eigenvectors for distinct central eigenvalues are linearly independent, by the usual argument with a shortest linear relation. Hence there are at most dimE​D bad values.

(ii) For λ=0 we have P+κ(λ)P′=κ(λ)(P′+κ(λ−1)P), and left multiplication by the central unit κ(λ) is injective and E-linear; apply (i) to the pair (P′,P).

Lemma 3.7 escape

PDF p. 9

Let W be a Goldie-torsion E-bimodule, 0=g∈W, 0=b∈R and Y⊆W a finite-dimensional E-subspace. Then grb∈/Y for some r∈R.

Proof in the paper

A basis of Y has a common regular annihilator c by the remark after Theorem 2.2, and Yc=0 because the actions commute. If gRb⊆Y, then gRbc=0. The set T={y∈R:gRy=0} is a two-sided ideal, proper because g=0, hence zero by simplicity. But bc∈T and bc=0 as c is regular.

Lemma 3.8 maximal rank

PDF p. 9

Let F⊆Z(R) be an infinite subfield, W a Goldie-torsion E-bimodule and κ:F→E a ring homomorphism with central image such that wλ=κ(λ)w for λ∈F and w∈W. Let P:D→W be an injective E-linear map with dimE​D<∞ and let 0=b∈R. Then there is r∈R such that v↦P(v)rb is injective.

Proof in the paper

We show that a map Pr​:v↦P(v)rb of maximal rank is injective. Each Pr​ is E-linear of rank at most dimE​D; choose r0​ with rankPr0​​ maximal, put Y0​=Pr0​​(D), and suppose 0=v0​∈kerPr0​​. By Lemma 3.7 with g=P(v0​) there is r1​ with w=P(v0​)r1​b∈/Y0​. Let j:Y0​→D be an E-linear section of Pr0​​. For λ∈F× the commuting actions give Pr0​+λr1​​(j(y)+μκ(λ)−1v0​)=y+μw+κ(λ)P(j(y))r1​b(y∈Y0​, μ∈E). The map (y,μ)↦y+μw on Y0​⊕E is injective, so by Lemma 3.6(i) the right side is injective in (y,μ) for some λ=0, as F is infinite. Then rankPr0​+λr1​​≥dimY0​+1, a contradiction.

Lemma 3.9 sections of torsion modules

PDF p. 9

If C is an e-critical Goldie-torsion module, then Γe​(C) is Goldie-torsion.

Proof in the paper

By Goldie’s theorem it suffices to show that the right ideal a={y∈R:w⋅y=0} of a section w is essential, and for this that it meets every yR with y=0, since every nonzero right ideal contains such a yR. Let 0=y∈R; we may assume w⋅y=0. Represent w⋅y by ψ:U→C with U⊆R an e-dense right ideal; as ψ=0, there is i∈U with c=ψ(i)=0, and (w⋅y)⋅i=ι(c) since both are represented by z↦ψ(iz)=cz. The map ι is injective, because cR=0 is not e-small; so yi=0. Choose a regular s with cs=0. Then w⋅(yis)=ι(cs)=0, so yis∈a∩yR, and yis=0 as s is regular.

§4 Choosing the element x+Ht

Definition 4.1

PDF p. 9

A test is a tuple (e,V,q,z,c) in which e≥0 is an integer, V a finitely generated Goldie-torsion module with KdimV≤e, q and z sections in Γe​(V) with q epic, and c∈R regular. An element f∈R satisfies the test if the section z+q⋅fc is epic.

A definition: the Lean statements of the results that use it unfold it.

Lemma 4.2 stability

PDF p. 10 · Lean graph

Let R be simple and right Noetherian with centre k.

(i)

If M is finitely generated with KdimM≤e, v∈Γe​(M) is epic and u∈Γe​(M), then v+uλ is epic for all but finitely many λ∈k.

(ii)

If f satisfies a test and g∈R, then f+λg satisfies it for all but finitely many λ∈k.

Proof in the paper

(i) Choose a critical series of M with top factors Ci​. For h∈Home​(M,Ci​), Lemma 3.5 gives h∘(v+uλ)=h∘v+ϕλ​∘(h∘u), so the map h↦h∘(v+uλ) is the pencil P+ϕλ​P′ of the ECi​​-linear maps P(h)=h∘v and P′(h)=h∘u into Γe​(Ci​). Here dimHome​(M,Ci​)<∞ and ECi​​ is a division ring by Lemma 3.3, and P is injective by Lemma 3.4. By Lemma 3.6(i) each pencil is injective for all but finitely many λ, and for the remaining λ Lemma 3.4 shows that v+uλ is epic.

(ii) For a test (e,V,q,z,c), as λ is central, z+q⋅(f+λg)c=(z+q⋅fc)+(q⋅gc)λ; apply (i).

Lemma 4.3 simultaneous tests

PDF p. 10 · Lean graph

Assume (S), (N) and (Z). For every x∈R, every nonzero t∈R and every finite list of tests there is H∈R such that x+Ht satisfies all of them.

Proof in the paper

We reduce each test to finitely many injectivity conditions on finite-dimensional spaces and satisfy them all at once, first for the factor Ht alone by maximal rank and pencils, then for x+Ht by one more pencil. Let k=Z(R) and let the tests be (ei​,Vi​,qi​,zi​,ci​). Choose a critical series of each Vi​ with Kdim≤ei​, and let α=(i,C) run over the pairs of a test and a top factor C of that series. Put Eα​=EC​, Dα​=Homei​​(Vi​,C), Wα​=Γei​​(C), bα​=tci​=0, and let Pα​,Zα​:Dα​→Wα​ be Pα​(h)=h∘qi​ and Zα​(h)=h∘zi​. Then Dα​ is finite-dimensional over the division ring Eα​ (Lemma 3.3), Pα​ is injective (Lemma 3.4), Wα​ is a Goldie-torsion Eα​-bimodule (Lemma 3.9; C is a subquotient of Vi​), and wλ=ϕλ​w on Wα​ with λ↦ϕλ​ injective with central image (Lemma 3.5). For H∈R, h∘(zi​+qi​⋅(x+Ht)ci​)=Xα​(h)+Pα​(h)Hbα​,Xα​(h)=Zα​(h)+Pα​(h)xci​, so by Lemma 3.4 the element x+Ht satisfies all tests if every map h↦Xα​(h)+Pα​(h)Hbα​ is injective. For r,r′∈R and λ∈k we have Pα​(h)(r+λr′)bα​=Pα​(h)rbα​+ϕλ​Pα​(h)r′bα​, as the actions commute.

Step 1. There is H0​ such that every map h↦Pα​(h)H0​bα​ is injective. We induct on the number of pairs. If H′ works for some of the pairs and, by Lemma 3.8, H′′ works for one more pair β, then for H′+λH′′ the map for each earlier pair is a pencil P+ϕλ​P′ with P injective and the map for β is a pencil with P′ injective. By Lemma 3.6 all but finitely many λ make all of them injective, and k is infinite.

Step 2. For H=λH0​ the maps h↦Xα​(h)+ϕλ​Pα​(h)H0​bα​ are pencils whose second map is injective by Step 1, so by Lemma 3.6(ii) all of them are injective for all but finitely many λ∈k. Choose such a λ.

Theorem 2.2 Goldie [23, Thms. 4.1, 4.4], [5, 2.3.5, 2.3.6]

Let R be a simple right Noetherian ring.

(i)

A right ideal of R is essential if and only if it contains a regular element.

The regular elements of R satisfy the right Ore condition: for every a∈R and every regular s∈R there are a′∈R and a regular s′∈R with as′=sa′.

Attributions the Lean proof does not use

Passages of the paper crediting results that no Lean declaration formalizes.

  • main.tex lines 222–229, citing [19] Stafford 1978

    When R/dR has finite length and R is simple Noetherian, Theorem A follows from [18, Prop. 1.3], which Stafford presents there as a special case of [19, Thm. 5.1], a theorem he attributes to Robson [19, p. 232]. Lemma 4.3 for a single test is close to the left-right mirror of [19, Thm. 5.1], which is stated there for simple left Noetherian rings and has no hypothesis on the centre; it lowers the Krull dimension once, with a prescribed factor, and each further drop costs a new generator [19, Thm. 5.5].

  • main.tex lines 677–682, citing [19] Stafford 1978

    For a single test the conclusion is close to the left-right mirror of [19, Thm. 5.1], which is stated there for simple left Noetherian rings and has no hypothesis on the centre; the central scalars serve to satisfy several tests at once.

  • main.tex lines 207–213, citing [14] Robson 1976

    Right ideals of a simple right Noetherian ring of Krull dimension n are generated by n+1 elements [13, Cor. 1.5], a bound Robson derived from cyclic objects in the quotient of the module category by modules of smaller Krull dimension [14, Def. 1.4, Thm. 4.3], using that such quotients of finitely generated modules have finite length, for which he refers to Gordon and Robson [15].

  • main.tex lines 365–370, citing [14] Robson 1976

    They play the role of the morphisms in the quotient of the module category by the modules of Krull dimension below e, in the sense of Gabriel [24, Ch. III], which Robson used to construct generators [14]; we work with them directly.

an epic germ v stays epic under v + u c for all but finitely many central c · statement of Lemma 4.2

Let R be simple and right Noetherian with centre k.

(i)

If M is finitely generated with KdimM≤e, v∈Γe​(M) is epic and u∈Γe​(M), then v+uλ is epic for all but finitely many λ∈k.

(ii)

If f satisfies a test and g∈R, then f+λg satisfies it for all but finitely many λ∈k.

Step 1 (a first element f). By P(e+1) there is H such that f=x+Ht satisfies L and J=I+fR has KdimR/J≤e.

Lean: step 1, line 104

Step 2 (torsion equation). By Goldie’s theorem there is a regular b with fb∈I (remark after Theorem 2.2). Then tb=0.

Lean: step 2, line 108

Step 3 (a correction g for the same ideal). The module R/J is Goldie-torsion, as s∈J, and KdimR/J≤e, so it has a unit test. Apply P(e+1) with x=0, the nonzero element tb and the list consisting of the unit test of R/J. This gives H2​ such that, with g=H2​t, the element H2​tb=gb satisfies KdimR/(J+gbR)<eandKdimR/Q≤e,where Q=I+gbR.(1)

Lean: step 3, line 111

Step 4 (an epic section modulo Q). Since I⊆J, we have J+gbR=I+fR+gbR=Q+fR. By (1) and Lemma 3.2 applied to Q, the section v=qQ​⋅f of R/Q is epic. Put u=qQ​⋅g.

Lean: step 4, line 120

Step 5 (a central scalar). By Lemma 4.2, applied to M=R/Q and to the tests in L, all but finitely many λ∈k make v+uλ epic and f+λg satisfy L. As k is infinite, choose such a λ=0.

Lean: step 5, line 126

Step 6 (inclusion). Put f′=f+λg and J′=I+f′R. Since λ is central, gbλ=f′b−fb∈J′,(2) because f′b∈f′R and fb∈I. As λ is a unit, gb∈J′, and hence Q+f′R=J′.

Lean: step 6, line 145

Step 7 (the dimension drops). As λ is central, qQ​⋅f′=v+uλ, which is epic. By Lemma 3.2, KdimR/(Q+f′R)<e, that is, KdimR/J′<e.

Lean: step 7, line 153

Step 8 (affine form). f′=x+(H+λH2​)t, and f′ satisfies every test in L. This proves P(e).
